He sat with that for a moment, his coffee gone cold beside the cutting board, the gate latch clicking shut out back. He did not think one method was true and the other false; he thought they answered the same question under different assumptions, and that you had to know which assumption the data had quietly violated.

He screenshotted both results, side by side, the empty grid and the seven names, and wrote underneath them a caption he revised twice before sending: same question, same data, different answers, and the blank is the whole story. He added the line he knew he would say out loud tomorrow: a single NULL in the list makes NOT IN return nothing at all.

Abygaelle replied first with a single word, rude but admiring. Nikola sent a voice note, mostly laughter, and then: bring it to Shin in the morning. Eric looked at the two windows on his screen a while longer, the way someone looks at a view from a montane trailhead before choosing which path to take, both of them descending into the same valley. Then he saved his notebook, closed the laptop halfway, and went outside to hold the flashlight for his father.

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: A footnote appears at the bottom of the page where the reference occurs, while an endnote collects the same kind of note at the end of the paper or chapter.
story:
The paper was due at eight the next morning, and Laura had forty percent of a bibliography. Ms. Ahmed had assigned it in September with what Laura now recognized as calculated patience: six weeks, a topic of genuine controversy, an argument that took a position, footnotes, and a bibliography in proper style. Laura had chosen coastal development, because her grandmother lived in a town where the marsh kept retreating and the county kept permitting. She had eleven sources, a thesis that had survived three drafts, and a word processor that had, sometime between midnight and one in the morning, decided to relocate every note in her document to the final page.

She had spent an hour the previous week formatting them. Each note sat, or had sat, at the bottom of the page where she had made the reference, numbered in the text with a small raised figure and matched below with the source. Now the pages ended clean and the numbers floated unmoored, and pages twelve through fifteen had turned into a solid column of notes. She highlighted one, dragged it back to the bottom of page four, and watched the program push it away again, down to the pile at the end, like a magnet repelling the wrong pole.

At seven in the morning she carried her laptop to the cafeteria, where Matis was eating hash browns and Puneet was copying lab data from her phone into a notebook. Laura opened the laptop between their trays. "Look at this. Is my paper broken?"

Matis leaned in. Puneet pulled the machine closer, scrolled, and scrolled again. "They're all on the last pages," she said.

"I know they're all on the last pages. They're supposed to be on their own pages. Each one is supposed to sit at the bottom of the page where I used the source. That's the whole point of them."

"Then it's broken," Matis said, and ate another hash brown.

Puneet was quiet for a moment. "Is it, though? My brother wrote a whole chapter of his thesis like this. Every note at the end, all together. He called them endnotes."

"Endnotes," Laura repeated. The word settled somewhere. She had seen it, she was almost sure, on a style guide handout, in a list of terms she had skimmed because none of them had seemed urgent.

"Endnotes," Puneet said again. "A footnote appears at the bottom of the page where the reference occurs, and an endnote is the same kind of note collected at the end of the paper or chapter. He said it both ways, like they were different options."

Laura looked at the column of numbers on the last page. The program had not mangled anything. It had organized them, sequentially, at the end of the document, all together, and the small figures in her text still matched the numbers in the list. It was not what she had built. It might still be what was required.

"Ms. Ahmed said footnotes," Matis said. "Specifically. She said the word footnotes like nine times."

"She also said a standard citation style. She said that more than nine times."

"You're going to equivocate," Matis said. "You're going to hand in something and then claim it's both things at once, depending on what she wants."

"I'm not equivocating if I actually decide which one it is."

There was no time to rebuild the notes at the bottom of each page. Laura did the arithmetic twice: six minutes to Ms. Ahmed's room, forty minutes until the deadline, and the process of dragging each note back and forcing it to stay would take more than forty minutes, if it worked at all, which it had not at one in the morning. She opened the style guide handout in her email, found the section she had skimmed, and read it properly. Footnotes at the bottom of the page where the reference occurs; endnotes the same kind of note collected at the end of the paper or chapter. The guide treated them as parallel forms. It did not say one was preferred. It did not say Ms. Ahmed preferred one.

"I'd just do the dragging," Matis said. "Clemency is for people who didn't have six weeks."

"That's not what clemency is for, and I didn't have six weeks, I had six weeks and a grandmother in a littoral county who sends me zoning-board minutes. The paper is about her coastline."

"It's very good," Puneet said, without looking up from the notebook, in the flat voice she used for true things she did not want to argue about.

Laura renamed a section heading at the top of the last pages: Notes. She checked the numbering, checked that each raised figure in the text still landed on the right note in the list, and checked the bibliography, which was separate and alphabetical and untouched. Then she wrote three sentences at the top of page twelve, before the notes began: that the notes in this paper appear together at the end, in order, each corresponding to the reference in the text; that the form is a recognized one. She read the three sentences and deleted the second one, because it sounded like she was asking to be forgiven, and she had not decided yet whether she had done anything wrong.

At 7:52 she was in the doorway of Ms. Ahmed's room. Ms. Ahmed was writing the due date on the board, though everyone in the room already knew it.

"Before you hand it in," Laura said, "I want to say something about the notes."

Ms. Ahmed turned around. Laura held the laptop out, open to page twelve, and said, "They're endnotes."

Ms. Ahmed took the laptop and read the top of the page.

"Every reference in the text has its number, and the note it points to is here, in order, at the end of the paper," Laura said. "Not at the bottom of each page. I know that's what you said. I'm asking whether this counts."

Ms. Ahmed was still reading. Laura watched her eyes move down the column of notes, past the source on littoral erosion permits from 2019, past the two newspaper pieces she had chased through microfilm, and stop at the note where she had cited her grandmother's letter. Ms. Ahmed closed the laptop halfway, folded her hands on it, and said, "The deadline is eight o'clock."

"I know."

"Then you have seven minutes to decide how confident you are."

Laura took the laptop back and stood in the doorway with the clock over the board showing 7:53, the printed copy already on the front desk with the endnotes inside it, and Ms. Ahmed returning to the board.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: Need-blind admission means a college decides whom to admit without considering whether the applicant can afford to pay; many US colleges are instead need-aware.
story:
The portal still said "pending" when Felix refreshed it at 11:58, though he had promised himself he would not refresh it again tonight. Two minutes felt like a reasonable exception, a loophole he drafted and ratified in the same breath. Behind the browser tab sat the spreadsheet he had been building since October, twelve colleges in a column, deadlines in another, and a third column he had left blank until tonight: whether the school looked at money when it decided.

He had spent the evening on the phone with his mother, who kept saying "your father will figure something out" in the voice she used when the opposite was likelier. Their contribution, according to the federal form, was going to be a number with a comma in an embarrassing place. Felix understood, in the abstract, that this was supposed to be fine, that aid existed, that bright poor kids crossed this bridge every year. In the specific, at his desk with the desk lamp making a small province of light, it felt less like a bridge than like a plank.

He called Alexane because she had already done the research, or said she had, and because she was the kind of person who read the fine print on things for pleasure. She picked up on the second ring, her face lit from below by her phone, a slice of pizza hovering into frame.

"Did you get anything," she said, before he could speak.

"Nothing. Listen, I need you to check something on my list. Some of these places, do they, I don't know, weigh whether you can pay? When they're deciding?"

Alexane set the pizza down, which for her was a gesture of gravity. "Some do, some don't. The ones that don't are need-blind, that's what it's called. They decide who to admit without looking at whether you can afford it." She tapped at her screen. "But a lot of schools are need-aware instead. They factor it in. Give me your list."

He read the twelve names aloud. She went quiet, typing, and the silence stretched long enough that he began composing apologies for the list itself, for having aimed so high, for the presumption of it.

"Okay, so, three of these are need-blind," she said. "And I mean actually need-blind, not the ones that say it and then have an asterisk the size of a thumb. The rest are mostly need-aware. Including, I'm sorry, Whitlock."

Whitlock was the one. Small, northern, a famous writing program, the place where a novelist he loved had gone and then written about going. He had written his application essay about his father's hands, about the way the knuckles had widened over twenty years of warehouse work, and he had felt, submitting it, like he was handing over something that was not entirely his to give.

"So my application to Whitlock is basically two documents," Felix said. "An essay, and an invoice."

"I mean, that's one way to problematize it." Alexane's voice was careful. "But it's not like they reject everyone who needs money. They admit some. They just look. You might still be one of them."

"That's the part I can't stand," he said. "Not the no. The not knowing whether the no, if it comes, is about the invoice."

She let that sit. On his screen the portal still said pending, a word that had begun to feel like a description of him rather than a status. He scrolled his spreadsheet and filled in the third column, need-blind three times, need-aware eight times, and one school he marked with a question mark because Alexane's sources contradicted each other. The completed column had a strange effect: it made the list look like a map of two different futures, one in which he was chosen for himself, one in which he was chosen against a budget line, and he could not make himself prefer the honest second one over the flattering first, because the first was not exactly honest either, since the need-blind schools were also the most competitive, and being rejected by them would tell him nothing about the money at all. Both columns were unpierceable. That was the tenable position he could actually defend to himself: that the information existed, that it was unfair in a direction he could name, and that naming it changed nothing about the waiting.

"There's one more thing," Alexane said. "My cousin applied to Whitlock two years ago. Need-aware. Full aid. She's there now, junior year, hates the winters, loves everything else." A pause. "So."

"So," Felix said. He almost laughed, the way you do when good news and bad news arrive wearing the same coat, when relief drops that far, that fast, into something smaller. He refused to call it hope; hope felt like bathos at this range, an epic swell for a kid at a desk lamp. He called it information and left it at that.

They hung up with the usual promises, talk tomorrow, tell me the second you hear. Felix closed the spreadsheet and then, because he could not close it, opened it again and moved Whitlock to the top of the list, where it had been before, where it would stay. The portal refreshed itself with a soft chime. He looked at it for a long moment without reading it, one hand already on his phone to call his mother, the other flat on the desk beside the warm keyboard.

activity: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
knowledge_domain: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
fact: A simple random sample of about 1,000 people gives a margin of error of roughly plus or minus 3 percentage points for the whole sample's results.
story:
The school paper's server logged its polls at exactly 11:03, and Nicholas had until midnight to decide whether the front page would say what 934 students thought about the uniform policy. He sat at his desk at home with the spreadsheet open, cursor blinking in the cell that read 52 percent in favor. Dayne's messages stacked up in the corner of his screen like a queue of people waiting to argue.

"52 percent," Dayne had typed. "Majority supports uniforms. Headline writes itself."

"934 isn't 1,000," Nicholas typed back, though he wasn't sure why the number mattered to him. It just looked wrong, like a receipt with an extra item. He'd sent the poll himself, to every student email the office would release, and 934 had answered. He tabbed over to the layout file, where the mock front page already read MOST STUDENTS BACK UNIFORM CHANGE, and felt something in his stomach go quiet and stubborn.

Leanne was the one who cajoled people into answering surveys at all; she'd stood in the corridor for three days offering to trade gum for completed questionnaires, and the response rate had doubled. He called her. "Do you think 52 percent means most students actually want this?"

"I think it means 52 percent of the 934 who answered," she said. There was a television on somewhere behind her voice. "Also Dayne wants me to tell you the printer deadline is midnight, not whatever you're doing."

He opened a new tab and searched for how pollsters knew what a sample could say. The first result that looked reputable was a page about survey sampling. He read a paragraph, then read it again, then called Leanne back. "Listen to this. A simple random sample of about 1,000 people gives a margin of error of roughly plus or minus 3 percentage points for the whole sample's results."

"Say the middle part again."

"Margin of error. Plus or minus 3 points."

She was quiet for a second, and he could hear her doing the same arithmetic he was doing. "So 52 could be 49. And 49 isn't a majority."

From Leanne's side of the conversation, in her kitchen with the television muted and her mother's crossword spread across the table, Nicholas sounded like a person defusing something small and round. She had known him since they were both bad at karate, and she knew this particular tone, the one that meant he'd found a rule and was deciding whether the rule outranked the deadline. "It's not just 52," she said. "It's anywhere from 49 to 55. They're all the same number as far as the poll can tell."

"So the headline's a lie."

"It's a headline," she said, and laughed when he made an offended noise. "Fine. It's a lie with a spreadsheet."

He tried to reach Ms. Sandhu, who had taught the statistics elective before leaving for a semester elsewhere, and got her voicemail twice. At 11:31 Dayne sent the layout with the headline in 48-point type and the word FINAL in the filename, which Nicholas found both funny and vaguely metamorphic, the way pressure turned ordinary stubbornness into deadline stubbornness. He typed his reply slowly, because the apportionment of the front page was, in the end, his call: one story would lead, and everything else got squeezed.

He called Dayne instead of typing. "We can't say most."

"We got 52 percent."

"From 934 people. If it were about 1,000, a simple random sample that size has a margin of error of roughly plus or minus 3 points. That's for the whole sample's results. So 52 really means somewhere from 49 to 55, and 49 is the wrong side of half. We'd be printing a coin flip."

Dayne's silence had the texture of someone rereading his own messages. "Okay," he said finally. "But the article's due at midnight and we need something."

"Poll splits students on uniforms," Nicholas said. "Subhead: results within the margin, roughly three points either way at about a thousand respondents. Then we run the interviews."

"That's a boring headline."

"It's a true one."

At 11:52 the final version uploaded, and Dayne's last message was a thumbs-up and a complaint about the death of journalism at the hands of math. Nicholas closed the laptop and looked at his darkened screen, where his own reflection sat in the place the poll had been. Leanne texted him a photograph of her mother holding up the finished crossword, all filled in except one square in the corner, and beneath it she wrote: "even the pros leave one blank sometimes."

He texted back a single question mark, then turned off the lamp.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Skimming means reading quickly for the general idea, while scanning means searching a text for one specific detail such as a name or number.
story:
The article was Spanish, photocopied and faint in the middle where the toner had run dry, and Mr. Sutton had given them eleven minutes to prepare a spoken summary. Alex read the first sentence word by word, translating each one against the margin of his notebook, and by the time he looked up, four minutes had gone. He was on the second paragraph. The article was five paragraphs long.

Across the table, Ariel had already turned her page over and was drawing a small owl in the corner of her notebook. Ian, beside her, kept stabbing at his phone under the desk in the way he imagined was subtle. Mr. Sutton drifted between the rows with his hands behind his back, pausing now and then to read over a shoulder, saying nothing, which was worse than saying something.

Alex went back to the beginning. He understood the general shape of it: something about a water project in a town whose name kept appearing, some official who had been accused of something, and an event, a meeting or a protest, that the article said was coming. The problem was that Mr. Sutton would want specifics. He always wanted specifics. Last week Alex had summarized a piece about a railway strike in three vague sentences, and Mr. Sutton had looked at him with a noncommittal nod and said, "Details, Alex. A summary without details is a weather report," and moved on, and Alex had spent the rest of the class pretending the remark hadn't landed.

"Eight minutes," Mr. Sutton said.

The clock over the door had a second hand that seemed to pause between ticks. Alex's dictionary was open on his lap, and he had used it six times already, and each time he lost the thread of the sentence and had to go back and rebuild it. He was reading the way he read English, except in English he didn't read word by word, he realized; his eyes moved in drifts and leaps and somehow the meaning assembled itself. Here, though, every word was a locked door.

Ariel leaned across the aisle. Her owl had acquired tiny feet. "What are you doing?"

"Reading."

"You're crawling. What do you actually need?"

"The date of the meeting. And who got accused of what."

"Okay," she said, "so don't read it. Skimming is reading fast for the general idea, and you don't even need that. Scanning is hunting through for one specific thing, a name or a number. You need the date. Scan for numbers. Just run your eyes down until something looks like a date."

"That's cheating."

"That's reading," Ariel said, and went back to her owl.

Alex turned the page flat and let his eyes fall loose and fast, the way he looked for his own name in a class list, not reading but sweeping. A number surfaced in the third paragraph, and then a name beside it, a name he'd already seen in the first line of the article, and suddenly the shape of the thing reorganized itself. The official hadn't been accused; the article said a report had exonerated him, and that was why the residents had called the meeting, because they believed the report was a lie. There was a word he hadn't looked up, a word that in this light could only mean mendacity, and he recognized it now as the article's whole argument compressed into one term. He had been three paragraphs deep in grammar while the point of the piece sat there waiting to be found.

"Time," Mr. Sutton said. "Ian, you first."

Ian gave a summary that was fluent, confident, and almost entirely about the wrong town, which Alex only knew because he'd found the right details by not reading. Ariel went second and was good, of course. Then Mr. Sutton said, "Alex," and Alex stood and gave the date, and the name, and the exoneration, and the accusation of mendacity underneath it, and heard his own voice make Spanish sentences that hadn't existed in his head eight minutes before. Mr. Sutton nodded slowly and said, "Better," which was not praise exactly, but it was not the weather report either.

Afterward, packing up, Alex felt the gain and its cost sit side by side. He had found what mattered in the article, but he could not have said, if anyone asked, what the third paragraph's first sentence meant, word for word. Ariel was zipping her bag. "See," she said. He put the photocopy in his folder, the faint blank stripe running through the middle of the page where he had never read at all.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A metronome marking of 60 means sixty beats per minute, exactly one beat per second.
story:
Maria set the metronome on the piano lid and dialed it all the way down, past 120, past 80, until the weight came to rest at 60. The passage she was practicing, the third page of the Chopin waltz her teacher had assigned, was supposed to fly, and instead it collapsed every time she reached the sixteenth-note run. Her mother called from the kitchen that the pendulum sound was going to drive her insane, and Maria said, honestly, that it might drive her insane first.

She had started piano in September, late by any standard. Her father had said that if she wanted it, she should have it, and so there was a rented upright in the living room where the bookshelf used to be, and there was Ms. Chatterjee, who came on Tuesdays and listened without flinching. Isabela had been playing since she was seven and had told Maria, with the bluntness of someone who had survived it herself, that the first year would lambaste her. "Not the teacher," Isabela had clarified. "The instrument. It just beats you up, and then one day it doesn't, and then it does again."

At 60, the metronome ticked once each second. Maria had not known that before tonight. She had assumed the numbers were arbitrary, like sizes of paper, but she had counted against the clock on the microwave, one full turn of the second hand, and the pendulum had struck sixty times. Sixty beats per minute meant exactly one beat per second. She said it out loud to the empty room, and it sounded less like a fact than a deal she was being offered.

The run that had been defeating her took about four seconds at that speed, which meant four clicks, which meant sixteen notes divided among them. She put her hands in position, played the first four notes on the first tick, the next four on the second, and heard, for the first time, where her fourth finger was landing late. It had been hiding inside the blur. Slowed down, the mistake had nowhere to go. She played it again. Again. On the ninth attempt her left hand found the shape without her watching it, the way a word stops being letters.

Reid texted her a photo of his history essay outline at nine, captioned "kill me," and she called him. He was writing about how two textbooks gave different accounts of the same battle, and his problem was that he could not decide which one to trust. "That's historiography," Maria said, because they had just covered the word in class. "The study of who wrote it and why. You're not supposed to pick one. You're supposed to say what each writer wanted." Reid said that felt like cheating, and she said she used to think so too, sitting there with the metronome between them, one hand resting on middle C.

She thought about it while she practiced. Her teacher wanted the passage fast, eventually; the score wanted it fast; the recording she loved wanted it fast. And the only way she had found to get there was to be slow on purpose, to accept sixty ticks a minute as a kind of truth, and then to earn her way back up. Maybe speed and accuracy were not opposites so much as two accounts of the same event, written by different hands. She wasn't sure that held up. She played the run at 60 until eleven, then moved the weight to 72, and the notes scattered like dropped coins.

The next Tuesday, Ms. Chatterjee sat on the bench beside her and listened through the waltz without stopping her. At the run, Maria kept it slow, deliberate, every note placed, and when she finished, Ms. Chatterjee said, "Interesting choice." There was no lambaste in it, no correction. "Where did that fingering come from?" Maria said she had found it at sixty, one beat per second, and Ms. Chatterjee nodded once and turned the page.

"You know the composer metrified this at a tempo you can't touch yet," she said. "That's not an insult. It's a fact about where you are, not who you are. Next week, 80." She wrote it in the notebook in her small even hand. On the walk home, Maria stopped at the rock shop on Calder Street to buy a birthday present for Isabela and stood for a while at the case of metamorphic stones, the ones that had been something else under pressure and heat and had come out layered, striped, new. She chose a piece of gneiss the size of a plum, and the cashier wrapped it in tissue paper, and she carried it home with the metronome still ticking somewhere behind her, one beat per second all the way down the block.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: Elisabeth Kübler-Ross introduced the five stages of denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance in her 1969 book On Death and Dying, originally to describe terminally ill patients facing their own death.
story:
Chase stood at the edge of his grandmother's living room holding a paper cup of coffee he had no intention of drinking. The folding chairs had been arranged in rows, and relatives he recognized only from holiday cards moved between them like people executing a choreography they had all rehearsed elsewhere. His grandmother's urn sat on the mantel beside a photograph of her at thirty, and the impossibility of connecting that laughing woman to the small bronze container kept destabilizing him, the way a stair missing in a dark hallway does.

Aydin found him by the bookshelf, where Chase had been pretending to study the spines. "You okay?" Aydin asked, though he must have known the question was useless, because he answered it himself with a shrug before Chase could.

"I keep waiting for it to hit me," Chase said. "The stages."

Belle appeared with two deviled eggs she clearly didn't want either, holding the plate like a shield. "My grandfather died in March," she said. "I waited too. Everybody kept saying, you'll go through denial, then anger, you'll bargain, then depression, then acceptance. Like a bus route." She set the plate down on the shelf between Saramago and a dictionary of birds. "I never felt any of them. I thought I was broken."

Chase had studied the same list for a psychology unit in the spring, copied it onto an index card, even. Denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance. He had assumed it applied to him now, to all of them standing in this room with their paper cups, and he had spent three days privately checking his feelings against the checklist the way you check symptoms online, finding none of them, concluding something was wrong with him rather than with the list.

Later, when the room had thinned to the aunts who insisted on doing dishes and the uncle who insisted on helping badly, Chase slipped into the small bedroom off the hallway, the one where he used to nap as a child while the adults talked. His grandmother's reading glasses were still on the nightstand, one arm folded under, as if she had set them down mid-sentence. He picked them up, and the smell of her hand lotion rose off the case, lilac and something waxy, and for a moment the grief arrived with a physical weight, and then it left again, and he could not have said which stage that was.

He found Ms. Saleh by the kitchen door, where she had come from across the street the way she had for twenty years, holding a casserole dish she refused to surrender. She had taught the psychology unit. He asked her, quietly, where the stages had come from.

"Kübler-Ross," she said. "1969. On Death and Dying."

But that was all she gave him, because her hands were full and the uncle was calling her about oven temperature, so Chase stood in the hallway with the title turning over in his head and understood, slowly, the way you understand a pun an hour late, that the book was about dying patients. Not mourners. The stages had been written to describe people facing their own death, and somewhere along the way the world had picked the list up and applied it to everyone standing around urns with paper cups, and the list fit them about as well as his grandmother's glasses would fit him, which was to say, it rested on the bridge and slid right off.

He went back to the living room and told Belle and Aydin this, standing by the mantel. "It was for the patients themselves," he said. "Terminally ill people facing their own death. Not us."

Belle looked at the urn for a long moment. "So I wasn't broken," she said, and it wasn't a question, and it was the pithiest thing anyone had said all afternoon, better than the eulogy, better than the pastor's oratory, which had been fine but had made his grandmother sound like a stranger.

Still, Chase thought, testing it, the stages weren't nothing. His grandmother, in the hospice in June, had raged at the nurse over a misplaced water cup, had said take me home and I'll stop smoking forever, had slept for two days without speaking. She had run the whole route herself. Maybe the map was true for the dying and merely borrowed by the bereaved, a borrowed coat, and maybe that was why it hung wrong on him. He could not decide whether that made the model smaller or larger, and he was honest enough with himself, standing there, to admit he couldn't.

Aydin raised his paper cup. "To the coat," he said.

"To the coat," Belle said, and touched her cup to his with a small click.

Chase looked at the photograph of the laughing woman at thirty, then lifted his cup and joined them.

activity: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
knowledge_domain: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
fact: An argument from silence draws a conclusion from what a source fails to mention; historians treat it with caution because writers record only what seems important to them.
story:
The archive occupied the back rooms of the old library, three of them, smelling of paper dust and radiator paint, and Paige had been coming every Tuesday since September with a folder of photocopies she refused to leave in the drawers. She wanted one thing: proof that the 1927 flood had put the town's auxiliary hospital under six feet of water, because her grandmother had told that story on her deathbed and Paige's mother had said, more than once, that Grandma exaggerated.

Mr. Nguyen unlocked the cabinet with the Kerrigan diary and set the box on the felt table. Mr. Kerrigan had been the hospital's bookkeeper in 1927, a man who wrote something nearly every day for forty years. If the flood had happened the way Grandma said, it would be here. Paige turned to October with her pencil flat on the table, the way the rules required.

Beside her, Jazmine photographed each page for the digitization project she'd proposed to the historical society, her actual reason for being there on a school afternoon. Jazmine wanted the society's summer fellowship, and fellowship applications went better with a finished project attached. She adjusted the copy stand lamp and asked, again, whether Paige had found it yet.

Paige had not. October 4th, Mr. Kerrigan recorded coal deliveries, a disagreement with the coal man, and the price of eggs. October 5th through the 9th, the same, with a note about his son's furlough from the army ending early. October 10th, nothing. October 11th, the words "wet week." Then eggs again. Paige went through November and December and then the whole of 1928, and there was no flood. There was no water in the wards, no boats on Main Street, no ruined mattresses, nothing her grandmother had described.

"There wasn't a flood," Jazmine said, squinting at the screen of her camera. "He was the bookkeeper. He'd have written it down. If the diary doesn't mention it, it didn't happen."

"That's an argument from silence," Arlo said from the microfilm machine across the room, without looking up. He'd been reading the 1927 newspapers for his own project on the auxiliary fire brigade, and he said it the way he said most things, flat, like a fact he'd paid for.

Paige asked him what he meant, and he shrugged and kept cranking the film. So she sat with it. An argument from silence. She said it to herself and looked at the diary, at the columns of eggs and coal, and thought about what a bookkeeper considered worth ink. Kerrigan wrote prices. Prices mattered to Kerrigan. A disaster that cost the hospital nothing but labor and that the county later reimbursed might not have been a price at all. A man records only what seems important to him, she thought, and the thought did not tell her whether the flood was real. It only told her the diary couldn't decide it. She went back to October and read every entry again, slower, and found, on the 11th, after "wet week," the line item: "mattresses, 34, county acct."

By then Jazmine had stopped photographing, because the lamp had flickered twice and Mr. Nguyen had come over to say the building's wiring was older than anyone in it. He looked at the page Paige had her finger beside, not touching, and then at the boxes on the shelf behind her, and said the society also held the county engineer's letters, uncatalogued, if anyone had the patience.

From the doorway, Jazmine watched Paige copy the mattress entry onto a card, and felt the familiar small sting of not being the one to find things. She had spent two months learning the collection's order, and this girl with the grandmother came in on Tuesdays and turned up what mattered. But the fellowship wanted initiative, not luck, and there was a way to have both. "I'll catalog the engineer's letters," Jazmine said, out loud, to Mr. Nguyen, before Paige could volunteer. "For the application. If she reads them after."

He agreed, and the letters came down, sixty of them, bundled in twine that had gone brittle.

The twist was in the fourth bundle, though it did not feel like a twist at first. The county engineer wrote to the hospital board in October 1927 about drainage, and in November he wrote again, apologizing for a rumor then circulating that the hospital had flooded, a rumor he called injurious, since in his professional opinion the water had never exceeded eight inches in the lowest ward. The rumor, he wrote, seemed to have transmuted from an incident at the auxiliary hospital in the next county, which had genuinely gone under. Paige read the letter twice, then a third time, because it did not say there had been no water, and thirty-four mattresses on the county account said something else again, and her grandmother had been eleven years old in 1927, standing in eight inches or six feet, remembering what a child remembers.

Arlo came over and read the letter upside down, and said that the newspapers reported eight inches too, in one paragraph, page six. "So your grandma was wrong," he said.

"No," Paige said. "There was water. There were mattresses. The story moved counties somewhere along the way. All three of those can be true."

Jazmine threaded the letters into folders and marked the box. "So what goes on your card? Flood or no flood?"

Paige looked at the diary, the letter, the newspaper citation Arlo had copied out, and wrote: water entered the lowest ward, October 1927; extent disputed; sources agree on mattresses, disagree on inches. She left the last line blank for now and said, "Somebody has to want to know before I can say more."

activity: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
knowledge_domain: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
fact: The 1930s Dust Bowl followed the plowing of the Great Plains' native deep-rooted grasses, which had held the soil, so when drought came the wind carried the topsoil away.
story:
The internship was supposed to be about data entry. Elliot had imagined it that way when he applied, anyway: a county extension office in June, a desk fan, a spreadsheet of rainfall figures he could half sleep through, and by August a letter from Mr. Kovalenko, the district supervisor, saying Elliot was dependable, which was the word colleges liked. What he had not imagined was being handed a jar of topsoil on his second morning and told to drive it out to a farm that had lost a quarter inch of it in one storm.

"Priya's riding with you," Mr. Kovalenko said. "She knows the county roads." Priya was the other intern, a girl from his school he'd spoken to maybe four times in three years, mostly about borrowing pencils. She sat in the truck with her boots on the dash and narrated the whole way: whose field was whose, which families were related to which, until the map of the county turned into a family tree. "Honestly, half these people are cousins," she said. "It's consanguinity out here. Look it up. It explains the potlucks."

The farm belonged to a man everyone called the farmer, no first name, as if he were a job title that had swallowed a person. He met them at the gate with his arms crossed, and Elliot understood within a minute that the jar of soil was an insult to him, a sample taken from his land by an office that had been sending him letters. "They want me to leave strips of grass through the field," he said to Priya, not to Elliot, as if Elliot were part of the furniture. "Grass. In a cornfield. My father plowed every blade of grass off this section and raised corn on it for forty years."

"My grandmother did the same," Priya said, "back in the thirties." The farmer looked at her then, really looked, and something in his face shifted. "Where was she?" he asked. "Western Kansas," Priya said. "Oklahoma line." He was quiet for a moment. "She ever talk about it?" "She called it the Dust Bowl," Priya said. "That's all she'd call it. She said the wind carried the topsoil away. They'd plowed up all the native grass first, the deep-rooted stuff, and when the drought came there was nothing holding the soil."

The farmer was obdurate after that, or seemed to be; he said the drought here wasn't that drought, said the office wanted cover for its own budget, said his father's ground had answered to no one and neither would his. But he walked the field with them anyway, all the way to the fence line where a strip of unplowed grass stood between his corn and his neighbor's, a strip maybe eight feet wide that he had never once mentioned in any meeting. Elliot noticed it and said nothing. Priya noticed it and said nothing. The farmer stood at the fence for a long time with his back to them.

That was Tuesday. On Thursday Mr. Kovalenko sent Elliot into the basement archive to box old files, and Elliot, who had wanted a real problem all summer and now had one, went looking instead. He found the 1955 soil survey, and folded inside it a letter from the farmer's brother, dated 1971, asking the office to survey the same field, and a reply saying the office couldn't act without the owner. The brother had wanted the grass strips. The farmer, then twenty-two and freshly in charge of the land, had torn out the fences along that boundary himself. There was no explanation in the file. There never was, in files.

Elliot sat on the basement steps with the letter in his hands and thought about how he'd spent a week treating the whole thing as a persuasion problem, as if the right combination of rainfall data and yield projections could beseech a man into changing his mind, when the actual obstacle was a dead brother and a fence. He thought about his own father, whom he'd been quietly overruling in arguments since he was fifteen, always certain that being right was the same as being owed agreement. He was less certain now. It was possible to have the science on your side and still be standing on someone's grief.

He took the letter upstairs anyway. He set it on Mr. Kovalenko's desk without a speech, and Mr. Kovalenko read it, folded it closed, and put it in a drawer, and said, "You didn't find that." "I found that," Elliot said. "Then I'm telling you the archive's a mess," Mr. Kovalenko said, "and you should keep boxing." But on Monday the letters to the farmer stopped coming, and in their place a single page went out: a cost-share offer, no conditions, grass seed at half price, available to anyone, worded so generally it could have been addressed to the whole county.

Priya thought it was a dodge. "So we just wait for him to volunteer?" she said in the truck on Friday. "That's not a plan, that's a vibe." Elliot said maybe a plan that assumed the man was stupid had already failed twice, and Priya said, "Twice?" and he told her about 1971, and she was quiet the rest of the way out to the farm, which for Priya was like a full confession. When they got there the farmer was on his tractor at the far edge of the field, working along the boundary where the old strip of grass stood. They couldn't tell from the road whether he was plowing it under or widening it.

They sat on the tailgate to watch. Priya opened the cooler and handed him half a sandwich, which felt like a truce, though he couldn't have said what the argument had been. The tractor came down the field line slow, then slower, then stopped, and the farmer killed the engine and sat there looking at the grass strip, or past it, at the neighbor's ground, at the horizon where the wind was picking up dust off somebody's bare field, a thin brown haze that rose and hung and would not settle.

He climbed down finally and walked over to the truck. He looked at the jar of soil Elliot still had on the seat, the sample from June, its water long gone cloudy. "You still carrying that around," he said. It wasn't a question. He picked up the jar and held it up to the light, turning it, and the fine particles inside lifted and swam, and he watched them a long time before he set it back down. "Come back Tuesday," he said. "I want to show you where my brother wanted the first strip."

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
knowledge_domain: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
fact: The Venona decrypts of Soviet intelligence messages, released by the US government in 1995, confirmed that Soviet spy networks had operated in the United States.
story:
The war memorial stood at the edge of the park where the town kept its older griefs, a granite obelisk with names from two wars and a bronze plaque added later, out of sequence, for Korea. Florence spread her notes on the low stone bench beside it because the library had closed at four and Curtis had insisted the light was better out here anyway. Kaelan sat cross-legged on the base of the monument itself, which felt to Florence like a small transgression, though she said nothing.

The problem was simple to state and impossible to settle. Mr. Schneider had assigned each of them two historians, one who argued that the Cold War grew mainly from Soviet expansion and one who blamed American overreaction, and had asked for a paper that weighed the claims against evidence. "Against evidence," he had repeated, tapping the assignment sheet, as though the word were the whole lesson. Florence had read both books twice and had a page of quotations that contradicted each other so cleanly it seemed rehearsed.

"Here's the thing," Curtis said, flipping through the pages she had handed him. "This guy, the first one, he says the spying was basically invented. Paranoid fantasy, mass hysteria, McCarthyism before McCarthy. And the second one says, no, there were actual networks, actual agents, and the fear had a real object."

"Both can be partly true," Kaelan said from the monument. He was eating sunflower seeds and spitting the shells into the grass, which Florence also chose not to remark upon. "People can be genuinely threatened and also paranoid. That's not a contradiction, it's just a mess."

"That's not an answer."

"It's not supposed to be an answer. It's supposed to be the truth."

Florence looked at the names on the obelisk. Someone had left a small plastic flag in a bracket at the base, faded to a pink that had once been red. She picked up the second book again, the one that took the Soviet threat seriously, and ran her finger down the copyright page, and then, because a suspicion had begun to form, picked up the first book and did the same.

"Wait," she said.

Curtis leaned over. "What?"

"The second book cites these cables. Messages between Moscow and its embassy that American cryptanalysts broke. He calls them the Venona decrypts." She said the word carefully, the way she had sounded it out alone in her room. "The U.S. government released them in 1995, and they confirmed that Soviet spy networks actually operated in the United States. Real agents, real names, real transmissions."

"Okay," Curtis said. "So?"

"So look at when the first book was published." She held the page out to him. "Before that. He couldn't have seen them. Nobody could have. Whatever he thought he knew about the spying, he was writing in the dark, and then the light came on fourteen years before I was born."

Kaelan stopped spitting shells. He came over and sat on the bench, reading over Curtis's shoulder, and for a while none of them said anything. A man walked his dog past the memorial and the dog paused to investigate the seed shells.

"That doesn't make him wrong," Kaelan said finally. "The evidence came out in 1995. It doesn't prove everything he said was false. It just means he couldn't have known this."

"Then what do I write? That one historian had a bad break in the timing?"

"You write what's true," Curtis said. "The first one couldn't see the decrypts. The second one could. That changes how much weight each one can carry. That's what Schneider means by evidence, I think. Not who's smarter. Who could know what, and when."

Florence felt something shift, less like an answer than like sediment settling. The two books had been floating in her mind like rival truths, refusing to touch bottom; now they had an order, an alluvial layering, the later one built on ground the earlier one had never stood on. And yet causality would not simplify itself for her convenience. A real spy network did not prove that every accusation was honest. Fear could have a genuine object and still be wielded cynically, could protect the country and ruin innocent people in the same motion, and thedecrypts settled one question while leaving the harder ones exactly where they were.

She began writing in the margin of her notes, small and fast. Curtis watched the pen move.

"You're going to cite it properly, right? The decrypts."

"Obviously."

"Because if you're going to say the first guy was blind, you have to show the dates. Otherwise you're just taking sides."

She stopped writing. He was right, and it cost her something to admit it, because the margin she had just filled already had the shape of a verdict, and the verdict would have to be smaller now, more careful, more honest. She crossed out a line.

Mr. Schneider came around the path with his afternoon walk, unexpected, a sweater over his shoulders though the day was warm. He saw the books and the notes spread on the bench and the three of them clustered like conspirators, and he slowed.

"Working on it, then," he said, not quite a question.

"Florence found something," Kaelan said.

"Did she," said Mr. Schneider, and kept walking, and Florence watched him go, and then looked down at the crossed-out line and wrote beneath it: remains uncertain.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: The Hindu festival of Holi falls on the full moon of the month Phalguna, usually in March, and begins with a bonfire the night before called Holika Dahan.
story:
Alexis had told Dina she would come to the movie, and Dina had already bought the tickets, and now Alexis was standing in her aunt's driveway with a bag of gujiya her mother had made and no plan for how to be in two places at once. The bonfire was being built in the back garden out of scrap wood and an old chair that her uncle had been meaning to throw away for three years. Her cousins were already stacking it higher than was probably safe.

"It's tonight," her mother had said that morning, as though this settled everything. "Holika Dahan. You know it's tonight."

Alexis did know, actually. She had looked it up two weeks ago, mostly to win an argument with Carolyn, who had claimed Holi was just the colors, the powder, the photographs everyone posted. Alexis had found the whole sequence and recited it back: Holi falls on the full moon of the month Phalguna, usually in March, and it begins the night before with a bonfire called Holika Dahan. Then the colors come the next morning. Carolyn had conceded with a shrug, which was how Carolyn conceded everything.

But knowing the schedule was different from being in it. Dina's movie started at seven. The fire would be lit at seven-thirty, when the moon was already up, full and low over the rooftops. There was no way to do both, and Alexis had so far managed the problem by not verbalizing it to anyone, including herself.

"You're on coconut duty," her cousin said, pressing a bag into her hands. The coconuts had to go into the fire, that much Alexis remembered from other years, though she had never been the one to throw them.

She texted Dina from behind the garage. Something came up. Family thing. Even as she sent it she could see how it would land, thin and evasive, the kind of message she herself hated receiving. Dina replied with a single question mark, and Alexis put the phone in her pocket and did not look at it again.

The relatives arrived in waves. Her aunt greeted everyone with an effusion that seemed to increase with each guest, hugging Carolyn's equivalent from every branch of the family, pressing sweets on people who said they had already eaten. A neighbour, Ms. Oyelaran, came to the edge of the driveway holding a bowl she wanted to return, and stayed, watching the woodpile with open curiosity.

"You light it on the full moon?" Ms. Oyelaran asked Alexis, since Alexis happened to be nearest.

"Full moon of Phalguna," Alexis said. "It's a month in the Hindu calendar, usually lands in March. The fire is tonight, and tomorrow morning is when everyone gets covered in color. That part is Holi proper." She heard herself sounding like the search results she had read to Carolyn, and shortened it. "Tonight is Holika Dahan."

"Bonfire first, chaos second," Ms. Oyelaran said, nodding. "That's a nice order."

Alexis's uncle circled the pile with a match, then another match, then gave up and used the kindling her younger cousin had prepared. The fire took on the third attempt and climbed fast, and the adults began to talk over each other about the story behind it, about Prahlad and the king and the aunt who burned instead of the boy, and Alexis stood near enough to hear three versions and no two alike. Her mother's version had a line Alexis liked, something about faith being fireproof, and Alexis thought it was the kind of epigram that sounded better the less you examined it, though she did not say so.

She threw her coconut when her turn came. It went in with a muffled crack and a smell of scorched husk, and her cousin applauded as though she had done something skillful.

Later, sitting on the old chair that had not, after all, made it onto the fire, Alexis took out her phone. There was a second message from Dina: I paid for your ticket. You owe me.

Alexis typed three beginnings and deleted them. The truthful answer was that she had chosen the fire, and had made the choice silently, without asking Dina, without asking her mother, without even admitting there was a choice until it was already made. She could not make that into a sentence that did not sound like an apology or an excuse, and she was not sure she wanted to apologize.

Her mother sat down beside her with two plates of gujiya and gave her one without comment. The moon was fully up now, and the fire had burned down to a red core with the coconuts black inside it.

"Dina's mad at me," Alexis said.

"Probably," her mother said.

"I'm going to give her the money tomorrow. And maybe some color, if she wants it."

Her mother bit into a guziya and watched the fire. "Take her the pink," she said. "Nobody uses the pink."

activity: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
knowledge_domain: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
fact: In a strike, employees refuse to work; in a lockout, the employer stops work by keeping employees out of the workplace.
story:
The automatic doors didn't open. Sarah stood in front of Millhaven Foods with her backpack on one shoulder and her name tag already clipped to her collar, and the doors stayed shut as though the store had gone blind. A sheet of paper was taped to the glass at eye level, and behind it the registers sat dark, the carts nested in their long silver rows. She read the paper twice. Due to a labour dispute, the sign said, this location is temporarily closed. Employees should not report for their shifts.

"You too?" Skylar came up beside her, hair still damp from the shower, holding her bus pass. "I thought maybe it was just my schedule app being weird." She pulled the door handle anyway, which did nothing, and then laughed at herself for trying.

Inside, at a folding table on the sidewalk, sat two people Sarah recognized from the deli and the stock room, older women she'd nodded at for a year without ever learning their names. A coffee thermos sat between them. One of them, Ms. Andersen from produce, waved them over.

"You're locked out, girls," Ms. Andersen said. "That's what this is. In a strike, we'd be the ones refusing to work. In a lockout, the company keeps us out instead. They shut the doors on us." She said it without heat, the way you'd report the weather, and handed them each a flyer about the contract the union had been negotiating. Wages, hours, the scheduling software that changed their shifts with less than a day's notice.

Sarah took the flyer and felt something uncomfortably like embarrassment. She had worked here since September, and she'd had only the vaguest idea that she was in a union, that three dollars a month came off her cheque for it, that the rules about her breaks and her paycheque hadn't simply fallen out of the sky. She had let the place desensitize her to its own machinery. The schedule app pinged, she obeyed. Her pay went up fifteen cents when the minimum wage did, and she'd thanked the government, never wondering who had asked the government first.

"I have rent," Skylar said quietly, on the curb outside. "Like, my portion of it. My mom counts on it."

"I know."

"Is there even a right answer here? If we cross the line, we're working, we're getting paid. If we don't, we're standing outside a locked door."

Sarah looked at the flyer folded into quarters in her hand, then at the two women at the table, who were laughing about something now, sharing a thermos cup back and forth. Ms. Andersen had once let her take home the day-end flowers that would have been thrown out, had showed her where the good avocados were hidden under the display. That was a person, not a door.

My mother says unions were how her father got his pension, Skylar said. My father says they're why everything's so expensive. Sarah smiled a little at that. Then she took out her phone and photographed the sign, the dark doors, the table, because it seemed suddenly like something worth keeping. She texted her assistant manager a question she already knew the answer to, and the answer came back in four minutes: shifts suspended until further notice, do not attempt to enter.

They walked to the bus stop together, and Skylar was quiet in a way that wasn't like her, her moods usually as mercurial as the weather in April. Sarah, drifting in a reverie of grocery carts and pay stubs, almost missed it when Skylar spoke again.

"There's a rally," Skylar said. "Saturday. It's in the flyer, that little part at the bottom. Customers who want the store to settle, workers from other locations." She held up her own copy, which Sarah hadn't noticed her taking. "I'm not saying I know everything about this. I don't. I just know I'm not crossing that line, even if the line was drawn for me."

Sarah thought about the fifteen cents, about the app, about the flowers Ms. Andersen had handed her over the produce case with a wink. She didn't know yet what she'd say if her manager called with an offer of shifts at another location. She might say no. She might not. But Saturday she could stand somewhere, and that was a start.

"I'll come," she said. "Saturday. Should I bring anything?"

Skylar smiled, and pointed at the thermos on the folding table. "Coffee. Those cups look small."

activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
knowledge_domain: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
fact: According to Acts 15 in the New Testament, a meeting of the early church in Jerusalem decided that non-Jewish converts to Christianity did not need to be circumcised.
story:
The argument started over potato salad, which was how most arguments started at Luke's family gatherings, though this one had deeper roots than mayonnaise. His uncle had been holding forth about how the Bible was either all true or all useless, and Luke, seventeen and unable to leave a thing alone, had said that didn't seem like the only two options. By the time the paper plates were cleared, the uncle had challenged him to prove it, and Luke, idiotically, had said he would, by Sunday, when everyone came back for his grandmother's birthday.

Monday morning he told Trisha and Jordon about it in the library before first period. "I said the whole thing doesn't have to be a package deal," Luke said. "And he said that's just picking and choosing, and picking and choosing means the rules mean nothing."

"That's actually a decent point," Jordon said, which was Jordon's way of being helpful.

"But it's not just my point. Somebody in the book itself had to have faced this. The first Christians were Jewish, right? All those laws. Then people who weren Jewish started joining. Somebody had to decide what applied to them." He pulled a school library Bible toward him across the table. Trisha, who was raised on nothing in particular, watched with the mild interest of someone at a zoo.

Mr. Addo passed by with his coffee and paused. "You have a debate coming up, Harrison?" He coached the debate team, and Luke was his least experienced member, the one who still wrote his cases the night before.

"Sort of a private one," Luke said.

"Then treat it like one. Don't argue what you feel. Argue from the evidence, and be honest where the evidence runs out." He moved on before it could become advice, which Luke appreciated.

Luke found it that evening, cross-legged on his bed with the book open on the floor in front of him. Acts, chapter 15. A dispute had broken out in the early church, people insisting the new converts had to follow the old law, and so a meeting was held in Jerusalem where the apostles gathered to settle it. Luke read the scene twice, then a third time, his pulse doing something unfamiliar. The meeting in Jerusalem, according to Acts 15, had decided that the non-Jewish converts did not need to be circumcised. They did not need to carry the whole old code with them. The decision itself was written down, with a few obligations attached, but the central thing was clear: the early church had held a debate, in the book, about which ancient rules still applied, and had ruled some of them no longer binding. Luke sat there feeling like he'd found a door in a wall he'd been told was solid.

He called Jordon. "It's in there. Acts 15. They had a whole council about it."

"Wait, the people who wrote it were arguing about it?"

"Not just arguing. Deciding. They changed the application and wrote down that they'd changed it."

"So your uncle's all-or-nothing thing," Jordon said slowly, "the book itself doesn't do that."

Tuesday and Wednesday, Luke built the case the way Mr. Addo had taught them, on index cards. He found the counterarguments too, because a case without them was a house without walls. The obvious one: if you can drop one rule, why not all of them, and who decides? He wrote it at the top of a card in capitals and stared at it for a long time, because it was a real question and he did not want to pretend otherwise. He tried out the argument on Trisha at lunch. She played uncle, arms crossed, relentlessly.

"So the book says some old rules stopped applying," she said. "Fine. Who gets to say which ones now? You?"

"I don't think it's about who," Luke said. "I think it's about how you decide. They didn't just shrug. They met, they argued from the text, they ruled. It's a method, not a free-for-all."

"And if two people use the method and land in different places?"

"Then they land in different places." He heard how weak it sounded and said it anyway, because it was true. "Maybe the honest position is that the book models arguing about the book. That's what it gives you. Not a tiebreaker, but permission to do the work."

"That's going to be a short speech," Trisha said, but she was smiling.

Sunday arrived with the smell of his grandmother's roast and the folding chairs already out on the lawn. Luke's uncle found him by the drinks table before Luke could find his nerve, which was probably better. "You said you'd prove it," the uncle said. "Prove what, exactly?"

"That the all-or-nothing choice isn't the one the Bible itself makes. Acts 15. There was a meeting in Jerusalem, the early church, and they decided the non-Jewish converts didn't need to be circumcised. It's right there. They debated which of the old rules still applied, and they decided out loud."

His uncle's mouth opened, then closed. A cousin drifted over. Somewhere behind Luke, a screen door banged.

"Show me," his uncle said, and went inside to find the book on the shelf.

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: The word 'mortgage' comes from Old French for 'dead pledge', because the pledge ends either when the debt is paid or when the property is forfeited.
story:
The elevator smelled of fresh paint and something faintly like vinegar, and the agent held the door with one polished shoe while Jake's mother stepped into the hallway first. The apartment was on the fourth floor of a converted warehouse, two bedrooms, one of which Jake was apparently meant to subsume into a study, though he had brought only a backpack and a notebook full of college brochures. The agent, a woman with a clipboard and a lanyard, recited numbers as they walked: the rent per month, the security deposit equal to one and a half months, due before move-in, non-negotiable.

"How much to buy it?" Jake's mother asked, running a finger along the window ledge where dust had gathered in the seam.

The agent flipped a page. "The owner is open to offers around four hundred and ten. You'd need a down payment, typically ten percent for a first-time buyer, and the bank finances the rest." She said the word "mortgage" the way she said everything else, briskly, as if it were a brand of appliance.

Jake stood by the window. Below, a man was locking a bicycle to a railing, testing the chain twice. Rhys had told him something once, in Rhys's grandfather's kitchen over burnt toast, and Jake had half forgotten it until the agent said the word. He took out his phone and typed it in, angled so nobody could see the screen. The result came up in small grey type. He read it twice, then put the phone away and kept looking at the bicycle.

His mother was doing arithmetic under her breath, the way she did at the grocery store. "Forty-one thousand for the down payment," she said. "Plus legal fees, plus the deposit if we rent first while we save. It's like paying twice to get in the door."

"That's normal," the agent said. "Renters pay the deposit, buyers pay the down payment. One comes back to you if the place is left clean. The other becomes part of the price."

"Part of it, and then the bank owns the rest of it for twenty-five years," his mother said. She was not asking a question. She moved to the kitchen and opened a cupboard, closed it. The hinges were silent. "And if I can't pay some month?"

"Then there's insurance," the agent said, "an indemnity the lender requires, so the loan is covered if something happens to you." She said it kindly, or as kindly as that sentence could be said.

Jake thought about the phone screen. Old French, the grey type had said. The word came from a phrase meaning dead pledge, because the pledge ended when the debt was paid, or when the property was forfeited. Dead either way. He had asked Rhys about it that morning at school, and Rhys had shrugged and said his grandfather called it that, "a dead pledge, that's the old word for it," and gone back to his sandwich. At the time Jake had thought it was just a morose old man's joke. Standing in the empty room, with the afternoon light making rectangles on the bare floor, it seemed less like a joke and more like a description of something nobody wanted to look at directly.

Emerick would say rent was throwing money away, that ownership built something. Emerick's parents had bought a house at twenty-six and mentioned it often. Rhys would say the opposite, that tying yourself to a bank for decades was the real trap, that renting kept you free to leave. Jake had agreed with both of them on different days, depending on which one he'd talked to last. Here, in the actual room, with the actual numbers on the clipboard, neither position held still long enough to stand on. His mother wanted a door she could paint. The bank wanted a promise that only ended one of two ways. Both of those things were true at once, and he could not make them line up.

"The second bedroom gets good light," the agent said. "Afternoon, all day in summer."

Jake's mother stood in the doorway of that room for a long moment. She put her hand flat against the wall, as though checking whether the building was steady, and then she asked what time the office closed, because the deposit, if she decided, would need to be in cash.

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: Alfred Cobban's 1954 inaugural lecture at University College London, published in 1955 as The Myth of the French Revolution, attacked the Marxist social interpretation.
story:
Jordyn would tell anyone who asked that she had the historiography essay completely under control, and by Wednesday of the second week she had said so to four different people, twice to Ann and twice to her father over dinner. This was not strictly true. What she had was an outline with three headings and a thesis she had copied from the whiteboard in Ms. Demir's room and then half erased, so that it read, in her notebook, "the Revolution has been read differently because." Because what, she had not decided.

Ms. Demir had circumscribed the assignment tightly: two thousand words on how interpretations of the French Revolution had changed since 1800, and the essay had to identify at least one moment when the received story was seriously challenged. "You cannot just list historians," she had said. "Show me the argument shifting." Jordyn had written the word shifting and underlined it, and felt, at the time, that she understood.

Ann wanted the mark more than she wanted almost anything. She had already ordered three books through interlibrary loan and kept them stacked on the corner of her desk like sandbags before a flood. "I'm doing the revisionists," Ann announced at lunch, unwrapping a sandwich. "The whole collapse of the Marxist thing. It's the strongest essay because it has a villain and a turn." Jordyn said she was doing the same turn, only better, and Ann looked at her the way she looked at people who claimed to have finished the reading.

Jordyn's draft began confidently. For decades, she wrote, historians believed the Revolution was fundamentally a social conflict, the bourgeoisie rising against a feudal order, and everyone agreed on this until historians suddenly began to question it in the 1970s. She liked the sentence. It had the shape of a story with a hinge in it, and hinges, Ms. Demir had said, were what made historiography readable. She typed 1970s with a feeling of genuine perspicacity, as though she had located the exact seam in two hundred years of argument.

Then she went looking for a quotation to nail the 1970s down. The school library kept the history journals in a back room that smelled of dust and radiator, and the librarian let her in on the condition she did not reshelve anything herself. Jordyn worked backward through the volumes, past the 1980s, past the 1970s, and found, in an issue from decades earlier, a review of a small book. The reviewer's tone was clipped, almost amused. The book was called The Myth of the French Revolution, and it had grown out of Alfred Cobban's 1954 inaugural lecture at University College London, published the following year. The lecture had attacked the Marxist social interpretation, and the reviewer noted that Cobban had done it in front of an audience that had come expecting a polite ceremonial occasion.

Jordyn sat with the volume open on her knees. Her draft said 1970s. The review said the challenge had arrived in 1954, in a lecture hall in London, from a man taking up a professorship. The 1970s, she understood slowly, were the aftermath, the flood that followed someone knocking out the first stone. She thought of Ann, who would know this already, who had probably known it since the interlibrary loan books arrived. Ann was not capricious about grades; she was systematic, which was worse, because it meant she would not miss things the way Jordyn missed things.

She found Ann in the corridor before last period. "When did the Marxist view first get seriously attacked," Jordyn said. "Just tell me." Ann looked at the ceiling, deciding whether honesty was worth the risk of sharing. "Cobban," she said finally. "1954, his inaugural lecture at University College London, published in 1955 as The Myth of the French Revolution. It attacked the whole social interpretation." Jordyn nodded as though confirming something she had suspected, which was the kind of thing she did, and Ann knew she did it, and let her.

That night Jordyn cut the 1970s sentence apart and rebuilt it. The challenge came earlier and quieter than the textbooks implied, she wrote, when Cobban stood up at his own inaugural and dismantled the interpretation his audience had brought with them, in 1954, before the argument had a name for its later combatants. Then she stopped. Because she still could not decide what she thought. The Marxist reading explained why the Revolution happened, and that explanation had organized a century of writing; Cobban's attack explained why that organizing story might be a myth, but it did not quite put anything durable in its place. She sat with both of them on the screen, cursor blinking between the paragraphs, unwilling to choose, and aware that the essay was due in five days and wanted a position.

She typed a third paragraph that began, This essay takes no final side, and then deleted it, because it sounded like surrender. She typed instead, The evidence permits two readings, and stopped again. Her father called something about tea from the kitchen. Jordyn saved the file without a title, went down the stairs, and said, "Ask me tomorrow."

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: A down payment is the part of a home's price the buyer pays upfront so less must be borrowed; in British usage it is called a deposit.
story:
Clara's laptop fan had been clicking for twenty minutes before she noticed it, which was how far gone she was in the numbers. The letting agency's email sat open behind her spreadsheet: renewal terms for the flat, reply required by Friday, four days from now, or the family would be out on a month's notice. The rent was going up by two hundred a month. Her mother had said "we'll manage" in the tone that meant the opposite, and then gone to bed early, leaving Clara with the arithmetic.

She had done something rash that afternoon. Between school and home she had walked into the bank on the high street, into the smell of carpet and quiet voices, and asked the adviser at the desk what it would take to buy a small flat instead of renting one. The adviser, a brisk woman with reading glasses pushed up into her hair, had asked about savings, about income, and then had said, "So the deposit is the first question." Clara had blinked. She had a renter's deposit already, one month of rent held somewhere in the agency's account, and she'd assumed that was what they were discussing. She'd said, "We already have a deposit, it's with the landlord," and the woman had laughed, not unkindly. "No, love, the deposit on the price. In Britain they call it that. The down payment." Clara had stood there feeling stupid, thanked her, and left with a pamphlet she hadn't opened until now.

She opened it on the screen beside the spreadsheet. The pamphlet said it plainly enough in its beige paragraphs: the buyer pays part of the home's price upfront, and borrows the rest. So the "deposit" at the bank and the "deposit" at the letting agency were almost opposites, the same word bent into two shapes. It reminded her of something her chemistry teacher, Ms. Nwosu, had said in the spring, back when Clara still thought she'd be doing sciences: carbon was carbon, but in one allotrope it was pencil dust and in another it was a diamond, and nothing about the atoms had changed. Money, apparently, worked the same way. The same ten thousand pounds was coal in one sentence and diamond in another.

Her video call chimed. Malika, hair tied up, kitchen light behind her. "Are you actually doing homework or are you doing the thing," Malika said, by which she meant the Clara thing, the taking-responsibility-for-adults thing.

"The thing," Clara admitted. She turned the laptop so Malika could see the spreadsheet. Two columns. One was the new rent, which her mother could pay if Clara took a Saturday job, which Clara had already arranged without telling her, which was its own problem. The other column was a purchase price she'd found on a listings site, and beneath it the borrowing, and beneath that the monthly figure that came out lower than the rent, which had given Clara a brief and visceral jolt of hope, the kind that sits in the stomach rather than the head. Then the first row: the upfront part, the down payment, the deposit-by-the-other-name. It was larger than everything her mother had.

"There's a grant thing," Clara said. "For first-time buyers. I found it tonight. But the applications close Friday too."

"Same Friday as the agency deadline?"

"Same Friday."

Malika was quiet for a moment, and Clara knew she was choosing between the friend who would say go for it and the friend who would say this isn't yours to carry. "What does your mum actually want?" Malika asked. "Not what she can afford. What she wants."

Clara looked at the second bedroom door, closed, the light off. Her parents had sold the old house three years ago, in the year everything came apart, and her mother had refused every conversation about it since. Clara had once tried to raise it, gently, the selling, the timing, whether it had been the wrong call, and her mother had said, "You're not going to absolve me, and you're not going to blame me, so let's talk about something else." At the time Clara had thought it was a wall. Now, in front of the spreadsheet, she thought it might have been a door her mother couldn't afford to open, because behind it was the person who had signed the papers.

"I don't know," Clara said. "I've been deciding for her all week and she doesn't know I'm doing it."

"So tell her."

Clara typed a new row at the bottom of the spreadsheet, a placeholder, no number in it, just the words ask her. She set her cursor blinking there. On the screen the two columns sat side by side, rent and purchase, coal and diamond, and she did not know yet which they could become, only that by Friday one of them had to be chosen by the person whose name would go on the form.

She unmuted and said, "If I tell her about the grant tonight, will you stay on the line while I do it?"

Malika pulled her headphones back on. "Dial her extension," she said. "I'm not going anywhere."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
