fact: The yellow first-down line shown on televised American football is computer-drawn; it was first broadcast on ESPN on September 27, 1998, by a company called Sportvision.
story:
The stadium smelled like mustard and cold air, and Levi's cousin Deja, who was nine, kept standing on her seat to see over the railing. Their uncle had gotten the tickets through work, four seats together and two more a row back, which was how Levi ended up next to Tiana and Aila while his mother and Ms. Girma, their old neighbor from down the hall, shared a bag of peanuts behind them. On the Jumbotron above the far end zone, the game replayed in giant color, and there, on the screen, the yellow line stretched across the grass.

"It's so bright," Deja said, squinting down at the field, then up at the screen. "How do they paint it so fast? It moves every play."

Levi looked where she was pointing. Down on the actual grass there was no line at all, only chalk marks and the hash of cleats. He opened his mouth to say he didn't know, then closed it, because saying he didn't know had started to feel like a habit he wanted to break before college started in three weeks.

"It's not painted," Tiana said, leaning over Deja's knees. "My dad talks about it every single game. It's a TV thing."

"Where'd it come from, though?" Deja asked, obdurate in the way of nine-year-olds, arms crossed now. "It had to start somewhere."

Levi took out his phone. He typed in the question, half expecting a fog of forum arguments, and instead the answer came up clean, which almost never happened. He read it twice, then turned the screen so Deja could see, holding it low so the sun didn't wash it out. "The line's drawn by a computer," he said. "The first time anybody saw it on TV was ESPN, September 27, 1998. A company called Sportvision did it."

Deja studied the screen. "Nineteen ninety-eight," she repeated, as if tasting it. "That's before I was born."

"Before any of us," Aila said. She'd been quiet, wrapped in her jacket, and Levi remembered her saying the night before that she'd only come because the dorm move-in was lonely already and she wanted noise around her. He'd thought that was a strange reason to sit in the cold for three hours, but sitting here now, with the crowd roaring at a fair catch of all things, he thought he understood it better.

"Wait," Deja said. "So the players can't see it? They're just running to a line that isn't there?"

"To them," Levi said, "it's not there at all. It's only for us." He found that he liked saying it, liked holding both things in his head at once, the field as the players knew it and the field as the broadcast made it. It was like an argument where both sides were right and the truth was whatever you were standing in. In his ethics class senior year, Ms. Girma had called that kind of back-and-forth a dialectic, two positions pushing against each other until something sturdier came out of it, and he'd written the word in his notebook without really feeling it. He felt it now, a little, watching Deja work through the idea.

Down on the field there was a flag. Holding, the referee announced, offense, ten yards, and a whole section of the crowd groaned as one animal. Deja booed with them, delighted, and Aila laughed, a real laugh that surprised even her, and Levi's mother leaned forward between the seats to ask Ms. Girma whether the penalty could exculpate the linebacker from the earlier touchdown, since the hold had happened before the catch. Ms. Girma said she had no idea, that she was there for the peanuts and the people, and Deja patted her arm as though she were the one who needed comforting.

The offense lined up again. On the Jumbotron, the yellow line slid eight yards closer to the end zone, smooth as a shadow moving, and Deja watched it go with narrowed eyes, no longer fooled but still tracking it, the way you watch a magician even after you know the trick. Third down. The quarterback barked, the ball snapped, and Deja grabbed Levi's sleeve without looking away from the screen.

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
knowledge_domain: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
fact: Mozart's works are identified by K numbers from the catalogue compiled by Ludwig von Köchel, first published in 1862.
story:
The music room smelled of valve oil and old radiator dust, and Brody had spread the photocopied score across two chairs pushed together because the piano lid kept sliding shut on it. Mozart, Piano Sonata, K. 545. The K had been bothering him for two days, but that was a smaller problem than the one in front of him: the assignment, due Thursday, required him to draw a bracket over the exposition, another over the development, another over the recapitulation, and defend each line in writing. His pencil hovered over measure twenty-two. He had a suspicion, not a certainty.

"You're doing the face," Carina said from the piano bench, where she was picking out the opening theme one hand at a time. "The face you do when the math problem has a typo."

"It's not a typo. It's a decision." He set the pencil down. "Listen to this part, tell me what you hear." He nodded at the bar where the second theme slid, briefly, out of the sunlight.

She played it, then played it again, and Rayyan, who had come in carrying two cartons of chocolate milk and no apparent reason to be there, set one carton beside Brody's elbow without comment. "I'll be the stupid one in the room," Rayyan said. "What does the K mean? It's printed on the programme from that concert we went to. K. five forty-five. I asked my sister and she said maybe kilo."

"Like kilogram?" Brody heard himself say, with more confidence than he owned. "Kilometre. Some numbering thing, I think. Mozart numbered them himself." He said it because it sounded plausible, because the person who knows about sonata form is supposed to know about the numbers too.

Carina stopped playing. "You think?"

"I don't think. I'm checking." He already had his phone out, thumbing past the school's sad wi-fi handshake, and the room went quiet enough that he could hear the radiator tick. He read. He read it twice. Ludwig von Köchel. A catalogue, compiled by Köchel, first published in 1862, long after Mozart was dead; the K numbers came from that catalogue, and that was how Mozart's works were identified, every piece with its K. He put the phone face down on the piano.

"So Mozart didn't number them," Rayyan said, watching his face.

"No. Somebody else did. Köchel. Eighteen sixty-two." He turned the phone over and slid it across the music rack so Rayyan could read it himself, which felt better than saying it again. "So everything has a K number because one man sat down and made a list."

"Proselytize later," Carina said, spinning back to the keyboard. "You still haven't told me what I'm listening for at measure twenty-two."

He tried to explain while she played. The exposition, he said, was where the movement introduced itself, first theme, second theme, everything in its home key; the development took those themes and dragged them through keys they didn't belong to, like taking furniture out of every room in the house and rearranging it on the lawn; the recapitulation brought it all home, the same themes in the same order, but changed by having been away. It was the least original thing he had ever said about music, and Carina seemed to like it anyway, because she played the passage three times and frowned in a concentrated, useful way.

"The bit where it goes dark," she said. "That's where I'd start the development."

"That's what I thought. But Mr. Zhao said there's usually a repeat sign at the end of the exposition, and there is, it's right there at the double bar. So the second theme, the dark one, is still exposition. It's just exposition in the wrong key." He bracketed measure twenty-two in light strokes, ready to erase. "Which is either a beautiful trick or the reason I fail this."

Rayyan had a congenital inability to sit still in chairs, so he was now standing at the window with the second milk carton, watching the parking lot. "Mr. Zhao's coming," he reported. "He's got his coffee and his slow walk. You've got maybe a minute."

Brody looked at the page. The trouble was that the two ways of thinking didn't agree. By ear, the dark passage felt like leaving home, like development. By structure, the repeat sign said exposition, and structure was supposed to be the skeleton you could trust your ears against. He thought about Köchel again, a man in 1862 deciding that a dead composer's chaos needed an order, deciding where the list began. Maybe the brackets on his own page were the same kind of act: someone choosing a line and calling it the truth. He drew the recapitulation bracket anyway, at the return of the first theme, and left a note in the margin: could be a false return. He underlined false twice.

Mr. Zhao came in with his coffee and the unhurried mannerism of a man who had learned decades ago that hurrying teenagers was counterproductive. He looked at the score over Brody's shoulder for a long moment. "You've marked the second theme as exposition," he said.

"The repeat sign's after it," Brody said. "But it sounds like development. I wrote both down. I'm not sure which one wins."

Mr. Zhao drank his coffee. "Thursday, then," he said, which was either mercy or a trap, and moved off to unlock the cabinet where the metronomes lived.

Carina played the passage once more, very quietly, the dark theme in the wrong key that was somehow the right key, and Brody sat there with his pencil not moving, and then Rayyan leaned over from the window and tapped the page. "You realize," he said, "your whole assignment has a K number of its own now. Number one. First thing Brody ever analyzed. Catalogued by Köchel."

"That's not how the catalogue works," Brody said, but he was already writing B. 1 in the corner of the page, small, in pencil, where it could be erased.

"Keep it," Carina said, and played the final chord.

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: At a Passover Seder, the youngest child able to do so traditionally asks the Four Questions, which begin 'Why is this night different from all other nights?'
story:
Autumn set the Haggadot around her grandmother's table the way she had seen it done for sixteen years, spine toward each chair, the wine stains from 2009 left deliberately on Great-Aunt Ruth's copy because nobody had the heart to throw it out. This year the head of the table was hers. Her grandmother was in Toronto with her sister, recovering slowly, and had said only, "You know it better than you think," which Autumn did not believe and which exhilarated and terrified her in roughly equal measure.

The apartment filled by six. Her parents arrived with the roast chicken and the matzo ball soup; her little brother came straight from robotics club, still smelling of solder; Justine, whose family had moved here from Lyon in August, came because her own parents were at a conference and because she had told Autumn, with the flat honesty of someone new, "I've never been to anything like this and I'd like to see it." Tyrese lived one floor down and had claimed an invitation the week before, on the grounds that Mr. Leblanc from 4B had told him Autumn's grandmother's brisket was a matter of public record.

The problem surfaced before the candles were even lit. Autumn had rehearsed the order of the Seder on the subway, murmuring karpas, yachatz, maggid under her breath, and she knew that somewhere in maggid came the questions. But the questions were not hers to ask. She had asked them herself once, at five, in a dress with strawberries on it, and afterward her grandmother had passed the duty down the line of cousins like a coin. What she could not remember was the rule, exactly, and her grandmother's phone went to voicemail twice while the soup steamed on the stove.

She retreated to the hallway with the Haggadah and found her brother already there, pacing between the coat rack and the bathroom door, mouthing something. "Why is this night different," he whispered, "from all other nights?" He stumbled on the Hebrew, started over, stumbled again.

"You don't have to do it," Autumn said, and heard how it came out, like an exit being offered.

"I do, though." He pushed his glasses up. "Grandma called yesterday. She said I'm the youngest now."

Then Autumn remembered, the way you remember a room you lived in: it was not about bloodline or about her at all. At a Passover Seder, the youngest child able to do it asks the Four Questions, and the asking is the hinge the whole evening turns on. Her grandmother had told her that years ago, in the kitchen, not as a lesson but as a complaint about some cousin who had mumbled. She had simply filed it and forgotten she owned it. Her brother had the first half of the duty now, and she had the second, the answering, the leading of everyone through a text old enough to be almost unsayable.

"Say them to me," she said. "Start again. I'm the whole table." He stood straighter and asked why this night was different from all other nights, and she answered him, and he did it again in Hebrew, and when he got it right the second time, Justine opened the bathroom door she had clearly been listening behind and said, "Do that again, I want to catch the words."

The Seder itself was imperfect. Autumn read the plagues with a turgid solemnity that made her father snort into his wine, and she lost her place during the Four Questions' answer and had to find it by the rustle of pages around the table, which was its own kind of instruction, because everyone leaned in to help. Tyrese asked about the bitter herb, and she explained the austerity of it, the deliberate taste of something harsh on a night of plenty, and caught herself halfway into her grandmother's cadence, as though the words had been handed over with the candlesticks. Justine asked why the questions were asked by the youngest, and Autumn said she thought it was so the answer would have to be given fresh, every year, to someone new, and admitted she wasn't certain that was the reason, only that it was what the evening felt like it was for.

Her brother asked his Four Questions with a wobble on the third one and a recovery that made Ruth's wine-stained copy flap in applause. When they reached the meal itself, the chicken slightly overdone, the soup perfect, Autumn looked down the table at her grandmother's empty chair and did not fill it in any way she could name. She texted a photo of the Seder plate, then put the phone face-down before any reply came.

After the afikomen was found, hidden behind the bookcase where their grandmother always hid it, her brother came to stand beside her at the sink while she washed the Kiddush cups.

"That was good," he said. "It sounded like Grandma."

"It didn't, though," Autumn said, and handed him a towel.

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969) held that advocating force can be punished only if it is directed to inciting imminent lawless action and is likely to produce such action.
story:
The marble steps of city hall were still warm from the afternoon when Xavier climbed them with his accordion folder, and he noticed, the way he had been noticing everything lately, that his hands were sweating through the folder's edges. Inside, the council chamber had been rearranged into a courtroom: three desks at the front for the judges, a podium in the well, folding chairs for the audience, which tonight meant two parents, a bored clerk, and Coleton, who had come to watch Xavier fail.

The assignment had seemed simple a month ago. Mr. Suzuki had distributed the case file in the school library: a mock dispute built around an angry speech given on the courthouse steps, a crowd that was already gathered and already furious, and the question of whether the speaker could be punished for it. Each student would argue one side and then, without pausing, turn around and argue the other. "It will emancipate you from the comfort of having an opinion," Mr. Suzuki had said, and Xavier had written it down because it sounded like something worth writing down, though he was no longer sure comfort was what he wanted to be freed from.

Charles-Edouard went first, for the state, in a gray blazer he had clearly borrowed from someone larger. He spoke about order, about the fragile peace of a city, about how speech that lights a match near gasoline is not merely speech. He was good. Xavier watched the three judges, who were law students from the university, lean forward, and he felt the peculiar vertigo of agreeing with an argument he was about to dismantle.

At the podium, Xavier laid out his notes and found that he did not look at them. He had read the precedent so many times that week that it had begun to feel less like a rule and more like a machine whose gears he could turn in his head. Brandenburg v. Ohio, 1969. The Supreme Court had held that advocating force can be punished only if it is directed to inciting imminent lawless action and is likely to produce such action. He said it slowly, letting each condition sit in the room, and then he asked the judges to hold the speech against it, piece by piece. Was it directed to inciting? Was the action imminent? Was it likely? Somewhere in the middle of the third question he realized the audience was quiet in a different way than before, the quiet of people actually following.

Then came the turn, which Mr. Suzuki had warned was the harder half. Xavier stepped back from the podium, took a breath, and became the state. He argued that the crowd was already assembled, already angry, that the speech had been aimed at it, that the distance between the words and the first thrown bottle had been measured in minutes. It surprised him how naturally the words came, and how little he had to lie to make them. That was the unsettling part. Both positions fit in his mouth at once.

In the audience, Coleton raised his hand during the open comment period, which was not really allowed, and asked whether Xavier actually believed either side or was just a revisionist about his own beliefs, rewriting whichever history was convenient. The judges laughed. Xavier felt his face go hot, and then, unexpectedly, he laughed too, because there was something true in the insult. "Both, honestly," he said. "Which is sort of the point."

The judges conferred in whispers while Xavier stood with his hands folded, studying the vestigial gavel sitting unused on the center desk, a leftover from the chamber's other life as a place where the council voted on parking permits. One of the law students finally looked up. "Mr. Xavier," she said, "you gave us the Brandenburg test and then argued that the speech failed every prong of it, and then you argued it passed every prong. Which is it?"

He thought about the speech on the courthouse steps, about the crowd, about the bottle, about the speaker's face that the case file described but did not show. He thought about how the word "likely" was doing so much work, how it could stretch or shrink depending on who was frightened. "The speech is directed at inciting and the action is imminent," he said. "Whether it's likely to produce it, I honestly don't know, and I don't think the Court knew either. That's the part that gets decided by whoever's counting the broken glass afterward."

The judges looked at each other for a long moment. The one in the middle began to write something down, and Xavier watched the pen move across the page, waiting to find out what he had said.

activity: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
knowledge_domain: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
fact: Long or repeated exposure to sounds at or above 85 decibels can cause hearing loss, and the damaged hair cells in the human inner ear do not grow back.
story:
Marcus had taken the job at Park Lanes because it paid eleven dollars an hour and because the manager let him run the soundboard on Friday nights, which felt less like bussing tables and more like being somewhere. The bowling alley had started hosting local bands in the back room, four or five hundred kids standing on concrete under speakers older than he was, and by the second show Marcus noticed that the drive home was quieter than it should have been. Not peaceful quiet. Filled quiet, a thin whine threaded through the silence of the car like a wire. He rolled the window down to check whether the sound was inside his head or outside of it, and when the November air came rushing in and the whine stayed, he turned the radio up instead.

He did not mention it to anyone. There was a syllogism sitting in the back of his mind, something like: he needed this job until August, this job involved the speakers, therefore he would deal with the speakers, and the reasoning felt airtight in the way that only reasoning about things you have already decided to do can feel. He kept a notebook on the soundboard for set lists and mic assignments, and in the margins he had started keeping a different kind of list, small observations he did not fully understand. Friday: whine lasted until Sunday morning. Saturday matinee, mostly kids' birthday parties, squealing and machinery but no whine. He wondered what made the difference, whether it was the birthday parties' squealing, which was loud in a scattered way, or the bands, which were loud in a dense and constant way, and he wondered whether his ears could tell the difference even when he could not name it.

The manager had excoriated a coworker named Danny for unplugging a monitor mid-set two weeks earlier, standing in the narrow hallway by the fryers and laying into him about professionalism while Danny stared at the floor, and the whole crew had absorbed the lesson: nobody questioned how anything at Park Lanes was done. Marcus filed his notebook observations accordingly, in the category of things you keep to yourself. But Jolene, who worked the bar and was in his stats class at school, wore these small foam things in her ears on show nights, cream-colored stems just visible in the dark, and one Friday when the headliner was doing their sound check she caught him staring and held up the little plastic case.

"You're running the board and you're not wearing anything?" she said. Not accusatory, more curious, the way she asked questions in class. "My mom's an audiologist. She'd have a stroke."

"Is it that loud in here?"

"She measured it with her meter once when she was picking me up. Over ninety-five, back by the board." Jolene shrugged, wiping down the tap handles. "Anything at eighty-five or above, long or repeated, that's where the damage starts. That's the line she gives everybody." She said it lightly, the way you'd say a family fact, like how much salt to put in pasta water, and then a customer waved at her and she moved down the bar, and Marcus was left alone with the number.

That night, after close, he sat in his car in the parking lot and looked it up on his phone, the lot empty except for the manager's truck and one flickering sodium lamp. It took him four minutes to learn what Jolene's mother had spent years learning. The sources all agreed, and the part that kept him sitting there with the engine off was not the threshold, eighty-five decibels, long or repeated exposure, which was Jolene's number exactly, but what it led to. The loud sound damaged the hair cells in the inner ear, tiny and irreplaceable, and they did not grow back. He turned the word over. Hair cells. It made his ears sound like something fragile and grassy, a lawn he had been mowing with the volume knob, and the image was so stupid and so precise that he read the sentence three more times. Somewhere in the fourth or fifth website he found the word for the whine, tinnitus, and it helped to have a name for it, the way it helps to have a suspect's name even before you've caught anyone.

The question that actually interested him, though, the one he turned over on the drive home with the radio deliberately low, was what his ears were worth against what the job was worth. He was saving for the deposit on a fall semester dorm, and the Friday shows paid time and a half. It would be easy to construct this as noble, even altruistic, taking the damage so that the money went toward something his parents couldn't cover, and it would also be a load of nonsense, because plenty of people ran soundboards without losing anything. There had to be a version where he kept the shifts and kept his hearing, and the version was sitting in Jolene's ears every Friday, forty cents of foam, and the fact that he had gone three weeks without trying it seemed, in the parking lot's honest light, less like toughness and more like not thinking.

The next show he wore them. The room felt farther away at first, the vocals slightly underwater, and he panicked for ten minutes that he couldn't do his job, until he realized he could still hear the feedback loop forming, a thinness before the whine, better actually, because he wasn't braced against the whole wall of sound. Liana came with two friends from her art class and found him at the board during the second set, and she leaned in to shout something, saw the earplugs, and touched her own ear in a question.

He dug in his pocket and pressed a spare pair into her hand, the foam still in its wrapper, still warm from being carried around all week. "Eighty-five decibels," he said, pointing at the speakers, then at his ear. "Just take them."

Liana looked at the little squashed foam cylinders in her palm, then up at the wall of speakers, then back at him. She rolled one between her fingers, and the band crashed into the last song of the set.

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: The First Amendment to the US Constitution, ratified in 1791, says Congress shall make no law abridging the freedom of speech.
story:
The gym smelled of floor wax and burnt coffee, and the voting booths stood along the far wall like a row of confessionals. Alexia had come straight from school with her mock court binder under her arm, because her mother was working the polls all day and someone had to bring her dinner at six, and because the gym's back tables, once the election workers had claimed their half, were quiet enough to think in. She spread her notes across a folding table beneath the basketball hoop: on the left, the arguments for the school that suspended a student for a banner; on the right, the arguments for the student who unfurled it.

Mr. Okonkwo, the neighbor who lived two houses down and served as an election judge every November, set a cup of hot chocolate in front of her without being asked. "You look like a woman with two devils on her shoulders," he said.

"I have to argue both sides," Alexia said. "That's the assignment. Tuesday I speak for the school, Thursday for the kid with the banner. Mr. Okonkwo, what if I'm only good at one of them?"

"Then you'll find out which one you believe," he said, and went back to his roster of voters.

She hadn't wanted this case. She had wanted the one about search and seizure, with its clean wrongs and rights. Free speech was murkier, and murk made her anxious in a way she couldn't quite name. She flipped to the transcript page Alix had photocopied for the whole team, the one with the amendment itself, and read it aloud under her breath because reading it silently let her skim past the words without weighing them. "Congress shall make no law abridging the freedom of speech." She said it twice more. It was so short. Forty-five words in the whole amendment, her textbook said, and only ten of them were about speech, and the amendment had been ratified in 1791, before gymnasiums, before public schools, before banners and suspension slips. She wondered whether that mattered, whether words could be too old for the things they were being asked to cover, or whether being old was exactly what made them cover everything.

The door chimed and Silas came in with his skateboard under his arm and a leaflet he'd clearly been handed outside. He dropped into the chair across from her and slid the leaflet over. "The guy at the table says the polling place shouldn't even allow campaign people within a hundred feet, but he's giving these out anyway. Is that legal?" He had a way of asking questions that sounded like challenges.

"That's election law, not my case," Alexia said. "My case is a kid who held up a sign at a school event and got suspended for it."

"So the kid's right," Silas said. "Obviously."

"Say that Thursday. But Tuesday I have to say the school was right, and mean it enough that the judges believe me." She turned her binder so he could see the two columns. "Here's the thing. The school says the banner disrupted the event. The kid says disruption isn't the test, that the First Amendment protects unpopular speech precisely because it's unpopular, because otherwise you're just protecting speech nobody minds." She heard her own voice getting faster, the way it did when an idea started to take shape without her permission. "If we only protect speech that stigmatizes no one and offends no one, we're not protecting anything. But if schools can't regulate anything, a principal can't run an assembly. There has to be a line, and the whole fight is over who draws it."

Alix arrived at six-fifteen, out of breath, carrying the coffees she'd promised and had nearly forgotten. She wanted to be the team's closing arguer; she'd told Alexia this three times this week, and tonight her leaflets were dog-eared with highlighting. "I found the compromise position," Alix announced, sitting down. "Student speech is protected unless it undermines the school's educational mission. That's my line and I'm keeping it."

"That's not a line, that's a rubber band," Silas said. "It stretches to whatever the principal wants."

"It's a mutualism," Alix said, jabbing her straw through the lid. "The school protects speech, speech respects the school, both sides get something. That's how things actually work, unlike whatever you believe, which is that everyone should just yell from a skateboard."

Alexia looked from one to the other and realized, with a small cold shock, that they had just performed her assignment for her. Alix arguing order, Silas arguing liberty, both of them certain, both of them partly right. She pulled a fresh page toward her and began writing, and for a while the only sounds were the chime of the door, the election workers calling out names, and her pen.

Her mother appeared at seven, on her break, still wearing the volunteer badge with her name crooked on it. "How's the homework?" she asked, and Alexia read her the sentence again, slower this time. "Congress shall make no law abridging the freedom of speech. Ratified 1791." Her mother nodded and said it was strange to hear it read out loud in a room where people were doing the thing it made possible, and then she was called back to check in a disaffected voter whose registration had lapsed and who was, the man announced, done with all of it anyway.

By the time the polls closed, Alexia had both openings drafted, one for each side, and neither of them felt like a lie. What she didn't have was the thing she'd assumed she'd find: a way to make the two sides meet, or a way to know which one she'd choose if she were the judge. She read both drafts once more, and Silas read over her shoulder, and Alix argued for a comma she wanted cut, and Mr. Okonkwo began stacking the chairs, and when he reached their table he tapped the binder and said, "So which one won?"

Alexia closed the binder without answering, and slid it into her backpack, and went to help her mother carry the ballot boxes out to the car.

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
knowledge_domain: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
fact: John Lewis Gaddis's 1972 book The United States and the Origins of the Cold War, 1941-1947 argued that neither side could bear sole responsibility, a view called post-revisionism.
story:
Jade spread the two library books on the kitchen table the way other people laid out cards for a trick she hadn't learned yet. On the left, a tattered volume arguing that the United States had provoked the Cold War through economic expansion and the atomic bomb. On the right, a textbook chapter claiming the Soviets had made conflict unavoidable by consolidating Eastern Europe. Somewhere between them was Mr. Lavoie's debate assignment, due Thursday: take a position on the origins of the Cold War and defend it with evidence. The problem was that she had read both accounts twice now, and each one sounded complete until she picked up the other.

Her mother put a mug of tea beside the pencil sharpener and said nothing, which was a courtesy Jade had learned to appreciate during exam season. The house was quiet except for the radiator ticking, and Jade bent over her notes, which had deteriorated into arrows and question marks. What if both sides were telling the truth, she wondered, and the truth was bigger than either of them?

She texted Jeremie, who had drawn the opposite assignment and was therefore, by the arbitrary logic of classroom pairings, her sparring partner. He replied that he'd found a historian who blamed neither side alone, some Yale professor whose name he'd forgotten, and that Jade should look it up herself because he was at work until nine. She frowned at the message. Blaming neither side sounded like refusing to pick, which was the academic equivalent of shrugging.

Francesco called a few minutes later, apparently alerted by Jeremie, and Jade put him on speaker while she opened her laptop. "Did you find the name?" she asked, typing cold war origins historian neither side responsible into the search bar. Francesco said he hadn't, but that Mr. Lavoie had mentioned a term in passing after class, something with "revisionist" in it, and that Jade, being the class's resident polymath, would surely track it down in half the time it would take him. She told him flattery had never once improved her search results, and he laughed, and she scrolled.

The name surfaced quickly: John Lewis Gaddis. His 1972 book, The United States and the Origins of the Cold War, 1941-1947, argued that neither side could bear sole responsibility for the conflict. Jade sat back. Neither side. Not the Americans alone, as the left book insisted; not the Soviets alone, as the right one claimed. She found a review essay that gave the view a label, and she wrote the word in her notebook and underlined it twice before she realized she was holding her breath.

"Found it," she said into the phone. "It's called post-revisionism." Francesco repeated the word slowly, like tasting something unfamiliar, and asked what that even meant. "It means the professor who wrote it thought both countries were responsible," Jade said. "Both of them, together." There was a pause on the line, and then Francesco said that sounded like a cop-out, and Jade, who had thought the same thing twenty minutes ago, opened her mouth to agree and found that she didn't.

She pulled the two library books toward her again and tried the idea against the evidence, the way Mr. Lavoie kept telling them to do. The left book pointed to American loans and bases encircling the Soviet Union. The right book pointed to Stalin's control of Eastern Europe. What if, she thought, these weren't rival explanations but overlapping ones, two people describing the same knot from opposite ends of the rope? She read a passage on the breakdown of wartime cooperation, then flipped to the other book's account of the same months, and the accounts rhymed more than she had first noticed. It wasn't that the facts conflicted; it was that each author kept spotlighting a different set.

The discovery enthralled her so completely that she didn't hear her mother come back in, and she jumped when the kettle clicked off behind her. She'd been taught since middle school to pick a thesis and defend it, and the habit felt axiomatic, so obvious it needed no defense. Now she wondered whether the stronger position was the one that could hold two causes in mind at once and still say something definite. Maybe responsibility wasn't a pie where giving the Soviets half meant taking half from Washington. Maybe it was more like two drivers approaching an intersection, each certain the other would yield.

When Jeremie got home at nine-thirty, she called him and read him the sentence she'd drafted for her opening: that the older historians had treated the question as a trial with a single guilty party, while the post-revisionist view treated it as a failure with two participants. There was a long silence on the line. "I was going to argue the Soviets were mostly to blame," Jeremie said. "I had my whole case built." He asked whether Gaddis really thought it was exactly equal, fifty-fifty, and Jade said she didn't think it worked like that; the book seemed to be about how responsibility could be shared without being split into neat fractions, and that the honest answer included admitting what stayed murky. She liked that part, actually. The uncertainty felt less like a gap than like a door left open.

She stayed at the table after the call, rearranging her note cards into a new order, the American evidence and the Soviet evidence side by side now instead of stacked against each other. Somewhere in the middle she slid a card with a question mark, for the parts no archive had yet settled. Her mother passed through on her way to bed and paused behind her chair. "Getting somewhere?" she asked. Jade considered the row of cards, the underlined word, the two books lying open and, for the first time all week, quiet. "I think so," she said, and sharpened her pencil.

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: When parallel parking, a driver usually reverses in from alongside the car in front, turning the wheel toward the curb first and then away as the car swings into the space.
story:
The cones at Harrington Driving School were the florid orange of traffic cones everywhere, and Faith had come to think of them as a small civilization with strict laws. Pull even with the front cone, her instructor Ms. Van Dijk had said on the first day, then do what you like, apparently. What Faith liked was turning the wheel away from the curb immediately, which produced a car parked diagonally across two imaginary vehicles, every time.

"You're crooked again," said Celina from the back seat, where she and Wilson sat through each other's lessons because the school charged less that way and neither of them had money. Celina said it without malice, the way you'd report weather.

"I know I'm crooked. I want to know why I'm crooked." Faith let the car settle and looked at the space between the cones, a gap maybe a car and a half long. Somewhere in this maneuver there was a fact she was missing, and it bothered her the way a wrong note bothers someone who can't yet read music. She understood steering. She understood reversing. What she couldn't see was how they were supposed to meet.

Ms. Van Dijk leaned over from the passenger seat, spun the wheel with one hand, and tapped the curb-side window. "Watch my hand," she said, and that was all she said. She reversed along the front cone with the wheel turned toward the curb, then, mid-swing, turned it back the other way, and the car slid into the space like it had changed its mind about leaving. She pulled forward and gestured at the empty spot as if presenting a magic trick she refused to narrate.

Faith sat very still. You came in from alongside, backwards, and you turned toward the curb first. Then, as the car swung in, you turned away. Two opposite turns, one after the other, and the second one existed only to fix what the first one had started. It was almost dishonest, the way the maneuver pretended to aim at the curb and then didn't. She thought of her mother, who called any compromise a betrayal of principle, and of Wilson, who argued at lunch that principles were just feelings wearing fancy clothes, reified by people who needed their preferences to look like laws. Faith had never been sure either of them was right. Maybe some things worked exactly like this: commit hard in one direction, then correct, and the correction wasn't a contradiction but part of the whole movement.

She pulled up even with the front cone. "Shut up, both of you," she said, not meanly. She reversed, wheel toward the curb, counting under her breath, and the rear end swung in; then, when the angle felt like too much, she turned the wheel away and watched the body of the car straighten itself against the curb as if pulling its own collar straight. She stopped. The car sat parallel, close, plausible. Nobody in the back seat said anything for a second.

"Okay," said Wilson, "that was actually clean."

"One," Faith said. "I've done it once." She was already aware of how little once meant. She'd done it slowly, thinking aloud, with a patient instructor and a closed course, and the test would be faster, and then there would be the actual world, actual cars owned by actual people who had not consented to be part of her education. And there was still the highway. Merging terrified her more than parking, because parking was a closed problem with cones for citizens, while merging meant fitting herself into a moving stream that didn't care whether she arrived. Wilson, who had passed his test in June, claimed merging was about confidence, which Faith suspected was advice people gave when they'd forgotten what it felt like not to know.

The highway lesson came that Friday, dusk coming on, the on-ramp rising ahead. "Get up to speed," Ms. Van Dijk said. "Match them. Signal. Take your gap." Faith accelerated, watching the mirror, the traffic a procession of headlights she had to read like handwriting. A blue hatchback in the right lane; farther back, a truck. She signaled. The truck slowed, just slightly, a courtesy or an accident, and she couldn't tell which, and there was no time to reify the question of whether the world was kind. She swung in. The car settled into the lane, doing exactly what everyone else was doing, anonymous at last, and in the mirror the cones of the school lot were nowhere, not even a dot of orange.

"Check your mirror again," said Ms. Van Dijk.

Faith checked. The truck was two lengths back and holding.

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: GIS data comes in two main forms: vector data uses points, lines and polygons, while raster data is a grid of cells, each holding one value.
story:
The laptop screen was the only bright thing for a hundred metres. Isabelle sat with her back against a log, the tent breathing behind her in the wind, and tried again to load the two files Mr. Popescu had sent before the trip ended. The city's flood map appeared first, then the housing layer, and immediately something was wrong. The flood map looked like pixels, thousands of little squares going pale blue to deep blue, while the housing map looked like drawn shapes, clean outlines of parcels and blocks. One was a grid. The other was geometry. She had assumed maps were maps, that they would just stack.

"You're doing homework here?" Zakk crouched into the firelight with two mugs. "We're in actual woods, Isabelle."

"Mr. Popescu said whoever finishes the analysis by Monday gets to present it to the planning office." She took the mug. "And I'm stuck."

Brady came back from the river trail shaking water off his hands, taciturn as usual after a long walk, and sat down without a word. He looked at her screen longer than she expected him to. "Why does one of them look like Minecraft?"

"That's the problem." She zoomed in. The flood layer kept breaking into squares no matter how far she went. The housing layer kept its edges, crisp and indifferent. She tried to click a parcel and the software selected it, gave her its attributes, an address, a year. When she clicked the flood map she got nothing she could grab, just colour wherever colour was. It was like the two files were written in different languages, and the software was politely pretending they weren't.

From the next site over, Mr. Popescu's voice carried through the trees, telling someone to keep the hatchet out of the dirt. He had warned them he would be two campsites down all weekend, close enough to ask questions but not close enough to answer them for free. Isabelle introspected for a moment, which she did when she was about to cheat, turning the intention over to see whether it was worth the shame, and decided it was. She stood up.

She found him crouched by his own fire, feeding it one stick at a time, a stoic silhouette against the last of the dusk. He listened to her describe the two files, the squares and the shapes, and did not reach for her laptop when she offered it.

Zakk, who had followed her over because he never liked missing anything, watched Mr. Popescu's face for a hint and got none. "So it's broken?" Zakk said.

"It's not broken," Isabelle said slowly, and the words arrived as she said them. "They're two kinds of data. The housing map is the one with points, lines and polygons. That's vector data. The flood map is the grid of cells, each cell holding one value." She heard it leave her mouth and knew it was right, the way you know a key has turned. "So they're both fine. I just didn't know what I was looking at."

Mr. Popescu put his stick in the fire. "Was that a question?"

"No."

"Then go back to your tent."

From inside the tent Brady heard them coming before he saw them, boots on pine needles, Zakk laughing at something, Isabelle's voice already halfway into the problem. He had unzipped the window flap to let the smoke smell out and the cold smell in, cedar and wet canvas and the river underneath everything. He had also, while they were gone, taken her laptop and moved it off the sleeping bag, because she always left it where someone would kneel on it. Now she crawled in and pulled it onto her knees without thanking him, because she hadn't noticed.

She set the flood layer to half transparency and dropped it over the housing polygons, and the map finally became one thing. The deep blue grid pressed down across the northern edge of the city, and underneath it, outlined and clickable, sat four hundred and some parcels with houses on them. She started counting the ones under the darkest cells, and stopped counting and made the software do it instead. The number came up and sat in the corner of the screen.

"Is that bad?" Brady leaned over, breath warm on her ear.

"That's people," she said. "That many houses, in the deepest blue, on a map nobody at the planning office has apparently put on top of the other map." She was aware she might be wrong about that last part; the overlay was hers, the interpretation was hers, and she could not yet say whether the city had done this work already and buried it, or never done it at all. That stayed open, and she let it.

Zakk pointed at the screen. "Can you make the houses red? Like, the ones in the flood part red."

"Tomorrow," she said. "The battery's at eleven percent." She closed the lid and the tent went dark except for the fire's glow through the fabric, and outside, somewhere down the river, something heavy stepped into the water and stopped.

fact: The first carbon dioxide reading at Mauna Loa, in March 1958, was about 313 parts per million.
story:
Amy had volunteered at the science museum for one summer and knew the building better than most of the staff, which was why Mr. Saleh handed her the clipboard on Tuesday morning and told her she would be running the climate gallery that weekend. The gallery had a new interactive board where visitors pressed a button to see infrared light bounce off a glass panel, and beside it a printed graph of carbon dioxide measured at Mauna Loa, rising in small annual zigzags up a long slope. Mr. Saleh's only instruction was that she should be able to answer questions. Then he went back to the workshop, where a machine was extruding lengths of plastic for a new display case, and left her with the graph.

Her homework, due Monday, was on the same graph. The assignment asked how much carbon dioxide had increased over the record, which meant finding the starting value at the left edge. She had guessed 280 because that number was in her notes from class, and Brenden had marked it wrong in red pen when they compared answers at lunch.

"Read the axis," he said. "Start where the line starts." Brenden had a reputation for mathematical acumen that he mentioned often, though usually after getting something wrong, so Amy did not take his word for it. She stayed late in the library with the graph enlarged on a screen and traced the first data point with her finger. It sat just above 310. The label under the axis said the record began at Mauna Loa, an observatory in Hawaii, and the first reading there, in March 1958, had been about 313 parts per million. She wrote it down three times so she would not lose it.

On Saturday she took her post in the climate gallery. The morning was slow. A man in a green windbreaker stopped at the interactive board and pressed the button four times in a row, watching the red line of light turn back on itself against the glass.

"So the gas is like this panel," Amy said, stepping closer than she meant to. "Sunlight comes through, the Earth warms up, and the warm surface gives off infrared, which the gas sends back down instead of letting it escape. The light doesn't leave."

The man looked at her, then at the panel, then pressed the button a fifth time. "Like a blanket," he said.

"Like a blanket you can see through from one side," she said, and felt the phrase settle into place, the way the class explanation never quite had. She had spent two days turning the textbook version over, testing it against the board, and the two accounts had finally joined.

At the graph, though, the man slowed down. He put his finger on the right edge, where the line climbed past the top of the scale. "Who says this is real," he said. "Some computer."

"It's measured," Amy said. "At a volcano in Hawaii. They started in March 1958, and the first reading was about 313 parts per million." She pointed to the left edge of the line. "Everything after that is instrument data, and it's been about a century of change, most of it in the last fifty years." She caught herself before adding anything about causes, because she was not certain which parts of the rise the instruments alone could account for, and she did not want to claim more than she could defend.

The man studied the left edge for a while. "Three hundred thirteen," he said. "All right. That part I believe." He tapped the glass over the zigzag pattern. "But before 1958? Nobody was standing there with a gauge. You don't know what it did before that."

Amy said that ice cores held older air, and he said ice was not a thermometer, and they stood there without either of them giving ground. She could defend the number. She could not defend the whole century, and she told him so, and he seemed almost pleased.

He wandered off toward the dinosaur hall, where the museum had built a wall of sedimentary rock in cross section, layers pressed flat and labeled in small brass letters. Amy turned back to the gallery. Mr. Saleh came through with a coffee and nodded at the interactive board.

"How's it going?" he said.

"Somebody believed the first number and nothing after it," she said.

"Better than yesterday," he said. "Yesterday nobody stopped at all."
